section.title: Two theorems about continuous functions
section.p: Continuity began as a local condition: x\text{ close to }a \implies f(x)\text{ close to }f(a). But local calm forces global behavior.
If a continuous graph starts below a line and ends above it, it must cross that line somewhere. If a continuous graph lives on a closed finite interval, it must reach an absolute maximum and minimum.
These facts sound intuitive from pictures, but their hypotheses are where the mathematical power lives.

subsection.title: Intermediate values
subsection.p: If the outside temperature is 50^\circF at sunrise and 74^\circF at noon, and changes continuously, it must pass through 60^\circF at some intermediate time. A continuous function cannot jump over intermediate values.

example.title: Finding a root without an algebraic formula

statement.p: Let p(x)=x^3-x-1. Then p(1)=-1\lt 0 and p(2)=5\gt 0.
Because p(x) is a polynomial, it is continuous on [1,2]. Therefore its graph must cross the x-axis at some point c\in (1,2), giving c^3-c-1=0.

figure.caption: A continuous graph that goes from negative to positive must cross the x-axis.

subsection.title: Bisection as a constructive proof idea
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem says a solution exists; bisection shows how to compute it numerically.

Midpoint m=1.25: p(1.25)\approx -0.297\lt 0, so sign change is on [1.25, 1.5].

subsection.p: The sequence of nested intervals [1,2]\supset [1,1.5]\supset [1.25,1.5]\supset \cdots traps a unique real number c by the Nested Interval Principle. By continuity, p(c)=0.

subsection.title: Why continuity is required
subsection.p: Define S(x)=\begin{cases}0, \amp x\lt 0, \\ 2, \amp x\ge 0.\end{cases} On [-1,1], S(-1)=0 and S(1)=2. The value N=1 lies between 0 and 2, but S(x) never equals 1 because it jumps.

figure.caption: Without continuity, a graph can jump over an intermediate value.

subsection.title: Highest and lowest values
subsection.p: A continuous function on a closed bounded interval must achieve an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.

example.title: Maximum and minimum on a closed interval

statement.p: Let f(x)=x(2-x) on [0,2]. This continuous function attains its absolute maximum 1 at x=1 and its absolute minimum 0 at x=0 and x=2.

figure.caption: A continuous function on a closed finite interval reaches its highest and lowest values.

subsection.title: Why closed and bounded intervals matter
subsection.p: Both hypotheses in the Extreme Value Theorem are essential:

row.cell: Values approach 0 and 1 but never reach them; no max or min.
Grows without bound in both directions; no max or min.
On [0,1], values get close to 1 but no max exists.

example.title: Proving \cos x = x has a solution

statement.p: Let f(x)=\cos x - x on [0,1]. Since f(0)=\cos 0 - 0 = 1\gt 0 and f(1)=\cos 1 - 1\lt 0 (since \cos 1\lt 1), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root c\in (0,1) with \cos c = c.
Some theorems guarantee that a desired quantity exists and is reachable before we develop formulas or algorithms to find it.

subsection.p: Continuity guarantees no skipped intermediate values and reachable extrema on closed bounded intervals. The next section examines warning examples where subtle traps arise.
